source.title: Bayesian interpolation with deep linear networks

record.tranche_reason: The paper derives test-error behavior for deep linear networks under Bayesian interpolation, using a theoretical risk analysis rather than the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper’s own Theorem 3.11 reports sample-wise test error as a function of the sample-to-input-dimension ratio. Double-descent findings cited from other work are not recorded as rows. It does not report model-size or epoch sweeps.
record.test_reason: Theorem 3.11 derives the expected squared test error of the optimal-feature-learning posterior, which deep linear networks reach, as the sample-to-input-dimension ratio α0 = P/N0 varies. This is a theoretical, non-empirical test of sample-wise double descent, i.e. whether more data can hurt near the interpolation threshold.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors state that the optimal-feature-learning posterior in a Gaussian data model shows sample-wise double descent in α0 = P/N0, with error diverging at α0 = 1, and present this as consistent with prior work [ZVTP22]. It is a corollary, not a main result.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses exact theoretical analysis of zero-noise Bayesian interpolation in deep linear networks, deriving expected test error under a Gaussian data model.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported error varies with α0 and label-noise variance σε².
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
record.problems: The test-error result is theoretical and specific to deep linear networks, zero-noise Bayesian interpolation, and the stated Gaussian data model. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

untested.parts: No sweep over model size; the error is evaluated only for the optimal posterior, which is independent of width and depth.
No training-time analysis; learning is Bayesian inference, not gradient descent.
Only an isotropic Gaussian linear data model under exact Bayesian interpolation; no empirical networks and no nonlinear data.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
λpost is introduced as an effective depth but is not used to predict the peak location.
Regularization tuning and the removal of the peak, and peak splitting into multiple descents, are not studied.

missing.what: The noiseless case σε² = 0 of Theorem 3.11, in which no peak occurs. It is implied by the formula but not recorded as a separate condition.

record.verdict_notes: The double-descent result is a short corollary. It reduces to the classical minimum-norm linear-regression bias-variance computation, because the optimal posterior is the same for every architecture. Depth and width therefore play no role in the curve. Neither original source is this paper. The tranche could arguably be T5, but the result agrees with the version, so T2 is kept.

versions.untested_parts: No test-error sweep over model size.
No test-error sweep over training epochs.
The result is for a specified Gaussian data model and optimal-feature-learning posterior, not a broad empirical survey of training-data regimes.
No capacity sweep across model classes; the reported sweep varies sample-to-input-dimension ratio in deep linear networks.
The paper introduces effective-depth measures and studies posterior quality, but does not show that one measure predicts double-descent peak location along size, epochs, and samples.
The error formula includes label-noise variance, but the paper does not test whether noise or regularization drives the peak, whether peaks split, or whether tuned regularization removes it.
No re-counting of complexity or test of whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Deep linear networks; optimal-feature-learning posterior N(µ*, νΣ⊥)
rows.size_stated: Output dimension 1; hidden widths not stated for Theorem 3.11
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate expected squared test error as the sample-to-input-dimension ratio α0 varies.

conditions.value: xi ∈ R^N0 ∼ N(0, I); yi = V0 xi + εi; ||V0||² = 1

rows.measure: Expected squared test error E_{x,X,ε}[|f(x) − V0 x|²]
rows.note: The authors state the error diverges at α0 = 1; this branch of the reported formula rises without bound as α0 approaches 1 from below, so increasing sample ratio near the threshold can raise error.
rows.check: The value is mis-transcribed. The proof in §4.9 gives the error as 1/α0 − α0 + σε²/(1 − α0) for α0 < 1, not (1/α0)[1 − α0 + (1−α0)^−1 σε²]. Either form diverges as α0 → 1⁻ when σε² > 0, so the state stands, but only for σε² > 0. With σε² = 0 the error 1/α0 − α0 falls monotonically to 0, so there is no peak. The row should state that the peak requires label noise, and it also bears on V6's noise-dependence part.

source_check.correct: For α0<1, expected squared test error = 1/α0 − α0 + σε²/(1−α0). Harmful sample increases near α0=1 require σε²>0.
source_check.locator_found: Theorem 3.11, §3.4.2; §4.9, final expression before the α0>1 case.
source_check.problem: The recorded parentheses incorrectly multiply the signal and noise terms by 1/α0.

rows.measure: Expected squared test error E_{x,X,ε}[|f(x) − V0 x|²]
rows.note: The reported formula decreases for α0 > 1 after diverging at the interpolation threshold.
rows.check: The formula σε²/(α0 − 1) is correct. It decreases past the threshold only when σε² > 0; with zero noise it is identically 0. The row also bears on V6's noise-dependence part.

source_check.correct: For α0>1, error = σε²/(α0−1). V3: reversed for σε²>0 because additional samples decrease error; absent for σε²=0. The formula supports V6's noise-dependence component. The theorem prints α0≥1, but the expression is undefined at equality.
source_check.problem: This branch shows post-threshold improvement, not an observed harmful sample increase under V3.

relationships.condition: Isotropic Gaussian inputs, linear teacher with label noise σε² > 0, optimal-feature-learning posterior (e.g. σ²=1 deep linear networks with L ∝ N)
relationships.reason: In r1 the error rises without bound as α0 → 1⁻, so more samples raise test error near the threshold. In r2 it falls as σε²/(α0−1) above the threshold.
relationships.display_finding: Error diverged as α0 approached 1 from below and decreased as σε²/(α0 − 1) above the threshold.

relation.reason: Theorem 3.11 derives the study's own sample-ratio-dependent prediction error and explicitly identifies double descent.

tranche.reason: Exact Bayesian analysis in Gaussian deep linear models tests sample-wise double descent through a different method.

source_check.notes: These are asymptotic theoretical errors for posterior predictions, including posterior variance; zero-noise inference does not mean noiseless training labels. This study supplies no empirical controls or uncertainty estimates; α0=1 is singular, and noisy α0>1 uses least squares rather than exact interpolation.
